content: Sucrose nephropathy, also known as osmotic nephropathy, IVIg-induced nephropathy, or hypertonic solution-induced nephropathy, is a condition associated with acute kidney injury (AKI) in high-risk patients, particularly those with preexisting renal impairment. This syndrome is most commonly observed in patients receiving intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIg) stabilized with sucrose. The condition was first described in 1942 by Rigdon et al., following the administration of intravenous hypertonic sucrose solutions. This discovery laid the foundation for the concept of osmotic nephrosis, a term used to describe histological findings of vacuolization in renal tubules after exposure to hypertonic solutions such as sucrose, hydroxyethyl starch, dextrans, or contrast media. Osmotic nephropathy later gained attention as a potential cause of contrast-induced nephropathy and, more recently, as a side effect of high-dose IVIg therapy. Notably, acute renal failure was not initially recognized as a complication of IVIg therapy when it was introduced in 1952. The first case of osmotic nephropathy linked to IVIg therapy was reported in 1987, and since then, numerous additional cases have been documented. The pathophysiology of osmotic nephropathy was initially elucidated through studies involving intravenous sucrose. Histological findings revealed swelling of proximal renal tubular cells and obstruction of the tubular lumen. With the introduction of sucrose-stabilized IVIg, sucrose nephropathy re-emerged as a significant cause of kidney injury. Various sugars, including sucrose, glucose, sorbitol, and maltose, have been used as stabilizers to prevent aggregation of IVIg molecules. However, more than 90% of IVIg-associated nephropathy cases have been linked to sucrose-stabilized preparations, which are the most commonly used in the United States. Sucrose, when filtered by the kidneys, is taken up by renal tubular cells via pinocytosis. Since these cells lack disaccharidase enzymes, sucrose accumulates within them, leading to the formation of vacuoles as vesicles coalesce. This process results in tubular cell swelling, luminal narrowing, and subsequent acute kidney injury. In contrast, sucrose-free IVIg preparations are associated with fewer reports of renal impairment, likely because alternative stabilizers can be metabolized by renal tubular cells. Patients with prior AKI due to IVIg therapy have been shown to tolerate sucrose-free IVIg well. Between 1987 and 2009, approximately 115 cases of sucrose-containing IVIg-induced kidney injury were reported in the literature. Risk factors for developing AKI in patients receiving sucrose-stabilized IVIg include advanced age, diabetes, intravascular volume depletion (especially in the context of diuretic use), and preexisting renal disease. The clinical presentation of sucrose nephropathy can vary widely, ranging from asymptomatic cases to significant renal impairment. AKI typically develops within a few days of IVIg infusion and is often characterized by anuria, resolving over several weeks. Chronic renal failure is exceedingly rare, with only one reported case in the literature. Management of sucrose nephropathy involves discontinuing IVIg therapy at the first sign of kidney injury. Early cessation of IVIg results in recovery of kidney function in more than 80% of cases. Treatment is generally supportive, similar to other forms of AKI, until renal function is restored. Approximately one-third of patients may require temporary hemodialysis. Preventive measures include close monitoring of urine output and creatinine clearance after initiating sucrose-containing IVIg therapy. Diluting IVIg preparations to reduce the sucrose load and ensuring proper hydration may help mitigate the risk of renal injury. However, studies on primary prevention strategies are currently lacking.
